claims.source: The biomechanical properties of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle have also been implicated in determining muscle spindle receptor potentials (Blum et al., 2017; Fukami, 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Poppele and Quick, 1985; Proske and Stuart, 1985), but intrafusal fiber forces have not been recorded experimentally in conjunction with muscle spindle afferent recordings, and only a few recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials exist (Fukami, 1978; Hunt et al., 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing experimental data.

claims.claim: Only a few recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials exist.
claims.source: The biomechanical properties of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle have also been implicated in determining muscle spindle receptor potentials (Blum et al., 2017; Fukami, 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Poppele and Quick, 1985; Proske and Stuart, 1985), but intrafusal fiber forces have not been recorded experimentally in conjunction with muscle spindle afferent recordings, and only a few recordings of muscle spindle receptor potentials exist (Fukami, 1978; Hunt et al., 1978; Hunt and Ottoson, 1975; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the scarcity of a particular type of experimental data, supported by citations.

claims.claim: In passive stretch of relaxed rat muscle, muscle spindle Ia afferent firing rates can be described in terms of extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank.
claims.source: We first demonstrated that in passive stretch of relaxed rat muscle, muscle spindle Ia afferent firing rates can be described in terms of extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the experimental work, demonstrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: In the relaxed condition, extrafusal muscle fiber forces provide a reasonable proxy for resistive forces of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle mechanosensory apparatus.
claims.source: In the relaxed condition, that is in the absence of central drive to the muscles, we assumed that extrafusal muscle fiber forces provide a reasonable proxy for resistive forces of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle mechanosensory apparatus (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is an assumption made for the passive stretch experiments.

claims.claim: Whole musculotendon force in rat experiments is not predictive of muscle spindle IFRs.
claims.source: We previously demonstrated that whole musculotendon force in rat experiments is not predictive of muscle spindle IFRs (Blum et al., 2019), and that only a portion of the total musculotendon force can be attributed to extrafusal muscle fiber force, with the remaining nonlinear elastic component attributed to extracellular tissues (Blum et al., 2019; Meyer and Lieber, 2011; Meyer and Lieber, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors and others.

claims.claim: Only a portion of the total musculotendon force can be attributed to extrafusal muscle fiber force, with the remaining nonlinear elastic component attributed to extracellular tissues.
claims.source: We previously demonstrated that whole musculotendon force in rat experiments is not predictive of muscle spindle IFRs (Blum et al., 2019), and that only a portion of the total musculotendon force can be attributed to extrafusal muscle fiber force, with the remaining nonlinear elastic component attributed to extracellular tissues (Blum et al., 2019; Meyer and Lieber, 2011; Meyer and Lieber, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Fine temporal details of rat Ia afferent firing in relaxed muscles could be reconstructed by linear combinations of estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank, subjected to a threshold.
claims.source: Like in cats (Blum et al., 2017), fine temporal details of rat Ia afferent firing in relaxed muscles could be reconstructed by linear combinations of estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank, subjected to a threshold.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 with experimental data.

claims.claim: Notable features of muscle spindle Ia afferent firing reconstructions include initial bursts, dynamic responses during ramps, rate adaptation during holds, and movement history-dependent firing.
claims.source: The notable features of muscle spindle Ia afferent firing reconstructions included initial bursts, dynamic responses during ramps, rate adaptation during holds, and movement history-dependent firing (Figure 2A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the figures showing model reconstructions of experimental data.

claims.claim: History-dependent initial bursts in Ia afferent firing coincide with large, history-dependent yank component in estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force.
claims.source: The reconstructions revealed history-dependent initial bursts in Ia afferent firing coincide with large, history-dependent yank component in estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B comparing the yank component to the initial burst.

claims.claim: The dynamic Ia afferent firing response during ramp stretches was primarily reconstructed by the force component.
claims.source: The dynamic Ia afferent firing response during ramp stretches was primarily reconstructed by the force component (Figure 2C) and was larger during the first stretch of a repeated sequence (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2C showing the force component contribution.

claims.claim: Rate adaptation during the hold period was reconstructed by the force component in both slow and fast stretches.
claims.source: Rate adaptation during the hold period was reconstructed by the force component in both slow and fast stretches (Figure 2C; Matthews, 1963).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Oxaliplatin Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reconstructed by the yank component, with a small contribution of the force component, suggesting a reduced sensitivity of the muscle spindle afferent to intrafusal muscle fiber force.
claims.source: These OX Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reconstructed by the yank component (Figure 2D, blue trace), with a small contribution of the force component (Figure 2D, red trace; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting a reduced sensitivity of the muscle spindle afferent to intrafusal muscle fiber force.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: When Ia afferents in healthy rats were perturbed through intra-axonal electrical stimulation and muscle stretch was applied immediately afterward, STIM Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reproduced by the intrafusal fiber force, with reduced sensitivity to the intrafusal fiber yank.
claims.source: Conversely, when we perturbed the Ia afferent in healthy rats through intra-axonal electrical stimulation (STIM; 500 ms duration, 100 Hz train of 30nA pulses) and applied muscle stretch immediately afterward (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 3), STIM Ia afferent firing phenotypes were primarily reproduced by the intrafusal fiber force, with reduced sensitivity to the intrafusal fiber yank (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The sensitivity of the muscle spindle Ia afferent to force and yank can be decoupled.
claims.source: Taken together, these data show that in the absence of changes in intrafusal or extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank signals, the sensitivity of the muscle spindle Ia afferent to force and yank can be decoupled and therefore may arise due to separate encoding or transduction mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of oxaliplatin and axonal stimulation on force and yank sensitivity.

claims.claim: Varying force- and yank-sensitivity generates diverse muscle spindle firing phenotypes similar to those observed experimentally.
claims.source: Varying force- and yank- sensitivity generated diverse muscle spindle firing phenotypes similar to those observed experimentally – including the OX and STIM phenotypes.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B showing the range of firing patterns produced by varying sensitivities.

claims.claim: Muscle spindle Ia afferent firing profiles exhibited larger initial bursts and dynamic responses as yank sensitivity increased, consistent with classically identified dynamic muscle spindle firing phenotypes.
claims.source: Under passive conditions, muscle spindle Ia afferent firing profiles exhibited larger initial bursts and dynamic responses as yank sensitivity increased (Figure 3B, left to right), consistent with classically identified dynamic muscle spindle firing phenotypes (Emonet-Dénand et al., 1977).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: High force sensitivity led to profiles with elevated plateau firing, consistent with classically-identified static muscle spindle firing phenotypes.
claims.source: High force sensitivity led to profiles with elevated plateau firing (Figure 3B, top to bottom), consistent with classically-identified static muscle spindle firing phenotypes (Emonet-Dénand et al., 1977; Jansen and Matthews, 1962, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: History-dependent muscle forces have been simulated previously based on muscle cross-bridge population cycling kinetics.
claims.source: History-dependent muscle forces have been simulated previously based on muscle cross-bridge population cycling kinetics (Campbell and Lakie, 1998; Campbell and Moss, 2000; Campbell, 2014; Campbell and Moss, 2002), but no current muscle spindle model has incorporated these principles, and thus none simulate history dependence in muscles spindle Ia afferent firing (Hasan, 1983; Lin and Crago, 2002; Mileusnic et al., 2006; Schaafsma et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claims.claim: No current muscle spindle model has incorporated cross-bridge cycling principles, and thus none simulate history dependence in muscle spindle Ia afferent firing.
claims.source: History-dependent muscle forces have been simulated previously based on muscle cross-bridge population cycling kinetics (Campbell and Lakie, 1998; Campbell and Moss, 2000; Campbell, 2014; Campbell and Moss, 2002), but no current muscle spindle model has incorporated these principles, and thus none simulate history dependence in muscles spindle Ia afferent firing (Hasan, 1983; Lin and Crago, 2002; Mileusnic et al., 2006; Schaafsma et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing models, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Muscle spindles contain bundles of specialized 'bag' and 'chain' intrafusal muscle fibers.
claims.source: Muscle spindles contain bundles of specialized 'bag' and 'chain' intrafusal muscle fibers (Boyd, 1962; Boyd, 1976; Boyd et al., 1977; Gladden and Boyd, 1985; Taylor et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Different intrafusal muscle fibers vary morphologically and mechanically, as well as in their contributions to Ia firing patterns, but their basic architectures are similar.
claims.source: While different intrafusal muscle fibers vary morphologically and mechanically, as well as in their contributions to Ia firing patterns, their basic architectures are similar (Banks et al., 1997; Banks, 2005; Banks, 2015; Gladden and Boyd, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Intrafusal muscle fibers are innervated by gamma motor neurons in two polar regions containing contractile muscle fibers, with an in-series non-contractile equatorial region around which the muscle spindle endings are wrapped and mechanotransduction occurs.
claims.source: Intrafusal muscle fibers are innervated by gamma motor neurons in two polar regions containing contractile muscle fibers, with an in-series non-contractile equatorial region around which the muscle spindle endings are wrapped and mechanotransduction occurs.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about muscle spindle structure.

claims.claim: Muscle spindle Ia receptor potentials and afferent firing are directly related to deformation of the equatorial regions.
claims.source: Muscle spindle Ia receptor potentials and afferent firing are directly related to deformation of the equatorial regions (Boyd, 1976; Boyd et al., 1977), which depends on the tensile forces in intrafusal muscle fibers.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The mechanistic muscle spindle model consists of a pair of half-sarcomere muscle models arranged in parallel, simulated using two-state actin-myosin population interactions.
claims.source: Our mechanistic muscle spindle model consists of a pair of half-sarcomere muscle models arranged in parallel, simulated using two-state actin-myosin population interactions (Campbell, 2014).
claims.evidence: This describes the structure of the model developed in this study.

claims.claim: The simulated 'dynamic fiber' loosely represented the putative dynamic bag1 intrafusal muscle fibers, thought to mediate muscle spindle initial bursts.
claims.source: The simulated 'dynamic fiber' loosely represented the putative dynamic bag1 intrafusal muscle fibers, thought to mediate muscle spindle initial bursts (Banks et al., 1997; Proske and Stuart, 1985; Schäfer and Kijewski, 1974; Schäfer and Schäfer, 1969; Song et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the model design choice, supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The simulated 'static fiber' loosely represented the bag2 and chain intrafusal muscle fibers of the muscle spindle thought to mediate tonic muscle spindle firing.
claims.source: The simulated 'static fiber' loosely represented the bag2 and chain intrafusal muscle fibers of the muscle spindle thought to mediate tonic muscle spindle firing (Figure 4A; Poppele et al., 1979).
claims.evidence: This describes the model design choice, supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The dynamic fiber model was designed with slower myosin attachment rates and with a more compliant passive element than the static fiber.
claims.source: The dynamic fiber model was designed with slower myosin attachment rates (Thornell et al., 2015) and with a more compliant passive element than the static fiber (Gladden, 1976) (see Materials and methods; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the model parameters, supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The mechanistic model predicted a spectrum of muscle spindle firing phenotypes identified in passive stretch conditions by varying the sensitivity (gain) of driving potentials to biophysically predicted intrafusal fiber force and yank.
claims.source: Our mechanistic model predicted a spectrum of muscle spindle firing phenotypes identified in passive stretch conditions by varying the sensitivity (gain) of driving potentials to biophysically predicted intrafusal fiber force and yank (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: History-dependent forces emerge within simulated intrafusal muscle fibers from cross-bridge population dynamics.
claims.source: As a result of our chosen kinetic scheme, history-dependent forces emerge within our simulated intrafusal muscle fibers from cross-bridge population dynamics (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C showing the cross-bridge dynamics.

claims.claim: When the muscle is at rest, the spontaneous formation and breakage of cross-bridges is at steady-state equilibrium.
claims.source: When the muscle is at rest, the spontaneous formation and breakage of cross-bridges is at steady-state equilibrium (Figure 4C, time 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C at time point 1.

claims.claim: As soon as a stretch is applied, the population of attached cross-bridges is also stretched, resulting in a short period of high-stiffness force response, known as short-range stiffness.
claims.source: As soon as a stretch is applied, the population of attached cross-bridges is also stretched, resulting in a short period of high-stiffness force response, known as short-range stiffness (Figure 4C, time 2; Lakie and Campbell, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C at time point 2 and supported by citation.

claims.claim: The scaling properties of muscle spindle dynamic responses and initial bursts with increasing velocity during passive muscle stretch arise from intrafusal cross-bridge kinetics.
claims.source: In our model, the scaling properties of muscle spindle dynamic responses and initial bursts with increasing velocity during passive muscle stretch arise from intrafusal cross-bridge kinetics.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding of the model, demonstrated in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The strain dependence of the cross-bridge detachment rates produces force profiles that contain linear increases in short-range stiffness and sublinear increases in force dynamic response as a function of stretch velocity.
claims.source: More specifically, the strain dependence of the cross-bridge detachment rates produces force profiles that contain linear increases in short-range stiffness and sublinear increases in force dynamic response as a function of stretch velocity.
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism by which the model produces velocity-dependent responses.

claims.claim: The model predicted a sublinear increase in dynamic index with stretch velocity, emergent from intrafusal mechanics, resembling the classically reported fractional-power velocity relationship in muscle spindle firing rates.
claims.source: We predicted a sublinear increase in dynamic index with stretch velocity, emergent from intrafusal mechanics, resembling the classically reported fractional-power velocity relationship in muscle spindle firing rates (Figure 5C; Houk et al., 1981).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Linear scaling of initial burst amplitude with stretch acceleration was predicted.
claims.source: In the same simulations, linear scaling of initial burst amplitude with stretch acceleration was predicted (Schäfer and Kijewski, 1974; Schäfer and Schäfer, 1969).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work showing this relationship.

claims.claim: Initial burst scaling was emergent from intrafusal muscle fiber yank at the onset of stretch due to the elasticity of attached cross-bridges that then detach rapidly after being stretched a small fraction of L0.
claims.source: Initial burst scaling was emergent from intrafusal muscle fiber yank at the onset of stretch due to the elasticity of attached cross-bridges that then detach rapidly after being stretched a small fraction of L0 (Hasan and Houk, 1975; Matthews and Stein, 1969).
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism for initial burst scaling, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Neither fractional-power velocity relationship nor linear acceleration scaling of initial burst has been previously demonstrated to arise from the same mechanistic model.
claims.source: To our knowledge, neither of these phenomena has been previously demonstrated to arise from the same mechanistic model.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model.

claims.claim: The biophysical model predicted history-dependent changes in the muscle spindle firing initial burst and dynamic response analogous to those previously reported in acute cat, rat, and toad experiments as well as in microneurographic recordings in awake humans.
claims.source: Our biophysical model predicted history-dependent changes in the muscle spindle firing initial burst and dynamic response analogous to those previously reported in acute cat, rat, and toad experiments as well as in microneurographic recordings in awake humans (Blum et al., 2017; Day et al., 2017; Haftel et al., 2004; Proske and Stuart, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6 and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: History-dependent features in the model emerged from the asymmetry present in strain-dependent cross-bridge detachment rates.
claims.source: In our model, these features emerged from the asymmetry present in strain-dependent cross-bridge detachment rates.
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism for history dependence in the model.

claims.claim: In three consecutive, identical stretches, the biophysical muscle spindle model predicted an initial burst and elevated dynamic response on the first, but not second stretch.
claims.source: In three consecutive, identical stretches, the biophysical muscle spindle model predicted an initial burst and elevated dynamic response on the first, but not second stretch (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the third stretch, the amplitude of the simulated driving potentials recovered asymptotically as the time interval between stretches increased to 10 s.
claims.source: In the third stretch, the amplitude of the simulated driving potentials recovered asymptotically as the time interval between stretches increased to 10 s (Figure 6A), resembling the recovery of spike counts during the dynamic response in rats (Figure 6B; Haftel et al., 2004) and the recovery of initial bursts as a function of hold period in toads (Figure 6B; Proske and Stuart, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and compared to experimental data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The model predicted an initial burst at the onset of sinusoidal muscle stretches, similar to that seen in microneurographic recordings from awake humans.
claims.source: Our model predicted an initial burst at the onset of sinusoidal muscle stretches (Figure 6C), similar to that seen in microneurographic recordings from awake humans (Figure 6C; Day et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and compared to experimental data.

claims.claim: A cross-bridge mechanism for history dependence has been proposed previously based on experimental findings.
claims.source: Although a cross-bridge mechanism has been proposed previously based on experimental findings (Haftel et al., 2004; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Proske et al., 1992; Proske and Gregory, 1977; Proske and Stuart, 1985), this is the first demonstration of history dependence in a muscle spindle model.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: This is the first demonstration of history dependence in a muscle spindle model.
claims.source: Although a cross-bridge mechanism has been proposed previously based on experimental findings (Haftel et al., 2004; Nichols and Cope, 2004; Proske et al., 1992; Proske and Gregory, 1977; Proske and Stuart, 1985), this is the first demonstration of history dependence in a muscle spindle model.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model.

claims.claim: Dynamic and static gamma motor neurons innervate the static and dynamic intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle, respectively.
claims.source: Dynamic and static gamma motor neurons innervate the static and dynamic intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: Simulated dynamic gamma drive increased the force and yank of the dynamic fiber during stretch, predicting increased receptor driving potentials underlying initial burst and dynamic responses, with proportionately smaller increases in baseline muscle spindle driving potentials.
claims.source: Consistent with many prior experimental findings, simulated dynamic gamma drive increased the force and yank of the dynamic fiber during stretch, predicting increased receptor driving potentials underlying initial burst and dynamic responses, with proportionately smaller increases in baseline muscle spindle driving potentials (Boyd et al., 1977; Hunt and Wilkinson, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Simulated static gamma drive primarily increased baseline muscle spindle driving potentials, and had much smaller effects on driving potentials underlying the initial burst and dynamic response during stretch.
claims.source: In contrast, simulated static gamma drive primarily increased baseline muscle spindle driving potentials, and had much smaller effects on driving potentials underlying the initial burst and dynamic response during stretch (Figure 7A–B; Crowe and Matthews, 1964a; Boyd et al., 1977; Crowe and Matthews, 1964b).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Previously reported increases and decreases in dynamic index as a result of dynamic versus static fiber stimulation, respectively, were predicted by the model.
claims.source: Even the previously reported increases and decreases in dynamic index as a result of dynamic versus static fiber stimulation, respectively, (Figure 7C left plot; Crowe and Matthews, 1964a; Crowe and Matthews, 1964b) were predicted by our model (Figure 7C right plot).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C and supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: When extrafusal muscle was activated to 50% with intrafusal activation at a nominal constant level, the stress in the extrafusal fiber increased, while the stress in the intrafusal fiber decreased.
claims.source: When extrafusal muscle was activated to 50% with intrafusal activation at a nominal constant level, the stress in the extrafusal fiber increased, while the stress in the intrafusal fiber decreased (Figure 8B, first column, top trace, purple and green traces, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The Ia afferent firing rate simulated using an integrate-and-fire neuron was abruptly silenced during extrafusal muscle contraction when intrafusal activation was held constant.
claims.source: The Ia afferent firing rate simulated using an integrate-and-fire neuron was abruptly silenced during extrafusal muscle contraction (Figure 8B, first column, middle trace); during this condition both the extrafusal and intrafusal muscle lengths decreased and tendon length increased (Figure 8B, First column, bottom trace, green-purple vs. orange trace).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: When intrafusal fiber activation was increased and extrafusal activation was held constant, there was no change in extrafusal stress or force, but an increase in intrafusal stress.
claims.source: In contrast, when intrafusal fiber activation (both static and dynamic) was increased and extrafusal activation was held constant, we observed no change in extrafusal stress or force, but an increase in intrafusal stress (Figure 8B, first column, top trace, purple and green traces, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: The increase in intrafusal stress caused an increased in simulated Ia afferent firing rate with no change in muscle fiber or tendon length.
claims.source: The increase in intrafusal stress causing an increased in simulated Ia afferent firing rate (Figure 8B, second column, middle trace) with no change in muscle fiber or tendon length (Figure 8B, second column, bottom trace).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: When concurrent alpha and gamma drive were simulated, Ia afferent firing was dependent on the relative balance of imposed shortening of intrafusal fibers by alpha drive and the activation of intrafusal fibers by gamma drive.
claims.source: When we simulated concurrent alpha and gamma drive, we observed Ia afferent firing that was dependent on the relative balance of imposed shortening of intrafusal fibers by alpha drive and the activation of intrafusal fibers by gamma drive (Figure 8B, third and fourth columns).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: If the extrafusal muscle shortening caused by alpha motor drive is not sufficiently counteracted by gamma drive, the Ia afferent will reduce its firing rate or cease firing altogether.
claims.source: Briefly, if the extrafusal muscle shortening caused by alpha motor drive is not sufficiently counteracted by gamma drive, the Ia afferent will reduce its firing rate or cease firing altogether (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: If the gamma drive to the spindle stretches the sensory region at a greater rate than the extrafusal shortening, the Ia afferent will increase its firing rate.
claims.source: Alternatively, if the gamma drive to the spindle stretches the sensory region at a greater rate than the extrafusal shortening, the Ia afferent will increase its firing rate (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: There is a set of extra- and intrafusal states that will lead to no change in Ia firing rate during isometric conditions.
claims.source: Finally, it follows that there is a set of extra- and intrafusal states that will lead to no change in Ia firing rate during isometric conditions (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: In experiments in human finger muscles, muscle spindle Ia afferents were shown to either increase or decrease their firing rates during an isometric contraction despite the same joint torque profile.
claims.source: We were inspired to use these observations to explain paradoxical Ia afferent firing rates from experiments in human finger muscles (Figure 8C; Edin and Vallbo, 1990), in which muscle spindle Ia afferents were shown to either increase or decrease their firing rates (Figure 8C, bottom traces) during an isometric contraction despite the same joint torque profile (Figure 8C, top traces).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: In the absence of gamma drive, the intrafusal fiber stress decreased as alpha drive increased resulting in no muscle spindle firing.
claims.source: As expected, increasing alpha drive decreased extrafusal muscle fiber length (Figure 8B, black trace), and increased extrafusal muscle fiber stress (Figure 8D, purple trace). In the absence of gamma drive, the intrafusal fiber stress decreased as alpha drive increased (Figure 8D, green trace) resulting in no muscle spindle firing as shown experimentally (Elek et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D and supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: When gamma drive was increased by a fixed amount, intrafusal fiber stress could increase, decrease, or experience no change in stress depending on the amount of alpha drive.
claims.source: When we increased gamma drive by a fixed amount intrafusal fiber stress could increase (Figure 8D, pink traces), decrease (Figure 8D, green traces), or experience no change (Figure 8D, purple traces) in stress depending on the amount of alpha drive.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: It was possible to generate almost any level of muscle spindle firing during isometric conditions where the muscle fibers shorten by varying the relative levels of alpha and gamma drive.
claims.source: As such it was possible to generate almost any level of muscle spindle firing during isometric conditions where the muscle fibers shorten by varying the relative levels of alpha and gamma drive.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the simulations shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: When the musculotendon was passive (no alpha drive), the muscle fiber length closely followed the applied musculotendon length.
claims.source: When the musculotendon was passive, i.e. no alpha drive, the muscle fiber length closely followed the applied musculotendon length (Figure 9A, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: When the extrafusal muscle fiber was activated during the stretch, there was a marked difference in musculotendon length compared to the applied length.
claims.source: Conversely, when the extrafusal muscle fiber was activated during the stretch, there was a marked difference in musculotendon length compared to the applied length (Figure 9A, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: In the case of the passive spindle, the musculotendon stretch in the absence of alpha drive produced a slightly higher muscle spindle Ia afferent response than in the presence of alpha drive.
claims.source: In the case of the passive spindle, the musculotendon stretch in the absence of alpha drive produced a slightly higher muscle spindle Ia afferent response than in the presence of alpha drive (Figure 9B, top row).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The baseline firing rate, initial burst, and dynamic response were all slightly larger in the case of the passive musculotendon compared to when alpha drive was present.
claims.source: Specifically, the baseline firing rate, initial burst, and dynamic response were all slightly larger in the case of the passive musculotendon.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: The addition of a tonic level of gamma drive increased the baseline firing rate, the amplitude of the initial burst, and the dynamic response to stretch in the passive extrafusal musculotendon unit.
claims.source: The addition of a tonic level of gamma drive increased the baseline firing rate, the amplitude of the initial burst, and the dynamic response to stretch in the passive extrafusal musculotendon unit (Figure 9B bottom row, green trace).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Adding alpha drive decreased baseline firing only slightly, abolished the initial burst, and had little effect on the dynamic response to stretch when gamma drive was present.
claims.source: Adding alpha drive decreased baseline firing only slightly, abolished the initial burst, and had little effect on the dynamic response to stretch (Figure 9B bottom row, purple trace).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: A diverse range of Ia afferent firing characteristics during passive stretch is emergent from first principles of intrafusal muscle contractile (cross-bridge) mechanisms.
claims.source: We demonstrated that a diverse range of Ia afferent firing characteristics during passive stretch – well-documented in the literature but not completely understood mechanistically – is emergent from first principles of intrafusal muscle contractile (cross-bridge) mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: Ia afferent firing in a broad range of behaviorally relevant conditions can be reproduced by converting the force and yank of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle into afferent driving potentials using a simple linear relationship.
claims.source: Ia afferent firing in a broad range of behaviorally relevant conditions can be reproduced by converting the force and yank of the intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle spindle into afferent driving potentials using a simple linear relationship.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated throughout the manuscript with various simulations.

claims.claim: The transformation from force and yank to driving potentials represents the yet unexplained mechanotransduction process in the equatorial encoding region of muscle spindle sensory organs.
claims.source: This transformation represents the yet unexplained mechanotransduction process in the equatorial encoding region of muscle spindle sensory organs.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of what the model represents.

claims.claim: Mechanical interactions within the muscle-tendon unit and forces external to the muscle all contribute to firing rates of muscle spindle Ia afferents.
claims.source: As such, mechanical interactions within the muscle-tendon unit and forces external to the muscle all contribute to firing rates of muscle spindle Ia afferents; they may even create firing patterns considered to be paradoxical if viewing muscle spindles as simple passive sensors of kinematic or kinetic variables.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulations in Figures 8 and 9.

claims.claim: The model provides a foundation for biophysically realistic, predictive muscle spindle models that can be extended to understand how properties of tissues, muscles, neurons, and central drive affect muscle spindle sensory function in health and disease.
claims.source: Importantly, our model provides a foundation for biophysically realistic, predictive muscle spindle models that can be extended to understand how properties of tissues, muscles, neurons, and central drive affect muscle spindle sensory function in health and disease.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the potential applications of the model.

claims.claim: The approach of starting with biophysical principles of muscle force generation enabled development of a muscle spindle model that predicts nonlinear muscle spindle firing properties beyond the conditions that it was designed to replicate, without any change in model parameters.
claims.source: Our approach of starting with biophysical principles of muscle force generation enabled us to develop a muscle spindle model that predicts nonlinear muscle spindle firing properties beyond the conditions that it was designed to replicate, without any change in model parameters.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the modeling approach and its advantages.

claims.claim: Other muscle spindle models do not exhibit history-dependence and either lack or always generate an initial burst at the onset of stretch.

claims.source: In our model, the initial burst emerges from the number of cross-bridges that are formed after a period of rest, temporarily increasing the stiffness of the fibers before being stretched to their mechanical limit.

claims.source: Our primary focus in developing our mechanistic model was to use the simplest two-state cross-bridge model of actin-myosin interactions to qualitatively, but not quantitatively, reproduce history dependence in its stretch responses (Figure 6A) as seen in biological Ia afferents (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: Despite discrepancies in the more abrupt stretch-shorten 'triangle' stretches, the model was able to closely reproduce the human Ia afferent response during the slow sinusoidal stretch.
claims.source: It should be noted that, despite the discrepancies in the more abrupt stretch-shorten 'triangle' stretches (Figure 6A), our model was able to closely reproduce the human Ia afferent response (Figure 6B,C) during the slow sinusoidal stretch, which may be more physiologically relevant.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of model limitations and successes.

claims.source: With our approach, it is impossible to separate the elastic contributions from endomysial tissue from those in myofilaments, from structures such as titin.

claims.evidence: This is a speculation about future model improvements, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The complex interplay between central drive, internal, and environmental forces cannot be ignored when decoding muscle spindle firing patterns, especially in voluntary movement and during interactions with the environment.
claims.source: Ultimately, it is clear that the complex interplay between central drive, internal, and environmental forces cannot be ignored when decoding muscle spindle firing patterns, especially in voluntary movement and during interactions with the environment.

claims.claim: Neuromechanical interactions are key in interpreting the afferent signals and percepts in a variety of conditions where mismatches in extrafusal and intrafusal mechanical state due to fatigue or pre-conditioning alter the perception of both force and position.
claims.source: Such neuromechanical interactions are key in interpreting the afferent signals and percepts in a variety of conditions where mismatches in extrafusal and intrafusal mechanical state due to fatigue or pre-conditioning alter the perception of both force and position (Proske et al., 2014; Proske and Gandevia, 2012), or the role of muscle spindles in perception of force and weight (Jami, 1992; Luu et al., 2011; Savage et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The multiscale biophysical model provides a new biophysical framework to move beyond the idea that muscle spindles can be characterized as simple passive encoders of biomechanical signals during movement.
claims.source: Our multiscale biophysical model provides a new biophysical framework by which we may move beyond the idea that muscle spindles can be characterized as simple passive encoders of biomechanical signals during movement, enabling a more sophisticated understanding of muscle spindles as proprioceptive sensors, their role in neural control of movement, and how neurological disorders disrupt sensorimotor systems.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the work.

results.result: In passive stretch of relaxed rat muscle, muscle spindle Ia afferent firing rates can be described in terms of extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank. Linear combinations of estimated extrafusal muscle fiber force and yank, subjected to a threshold, reconstruct fine temporal details of rat Ia afferent firing including initial bursts, dynamic responses, rate adaptation, and movement history-dependent firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C22 collectively demonstrate that muscle fiber force and yank can reconstruct diverse passive features of rat muscle spindle firing. The experimental data in Figures 1 and 2 show strong correlations between the force/yank model and recorded firing rates, with specific features (initial bursts, dynamic responses, rate adaptation) attributed to specific components (yank vs. force). The assumption in C15 is reasonable for passive conditions and the approach is validated across multiple afferents.

results.result: The sensitivity of muscle spindle Ia afferents to force and yank can be decoupled, as demonstrated by differential effects of oxaliplatin treatment and axonal stimulation. Varying force and yank sensitivity generates a spectrum of firing phenotypes resembling experimentally observed static and dynamic muscle spindle responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 are well-supported by experimental manipulations (oxaliplatin and axonal stimulation) that selectively alter force vs. yank sensitivity, and by systematic modeling showing that varying these sensitivities reproduces the continuum of static-to-dynamic firing phenotypes observed experimentally. The data in Figures 2D-F and Figure 3 provide converging evidence for independent force and yank encoding mechanisms.

results.result: A biophysical muscle spindle model based on cross-bridge cycling kinetics of intrafusal muscle fibers predicts well-known firing characteristics. The model consists of parallel 'dynamic' and 'static' fibers with different myosin kinetics, and history-dependent forces emerge from cross-bridge population dynamics including short-range stiffness.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C36-C43 describe the core biophysical model structure and demonstrate that it produces history-dependent forces from first principles. The model design is justified by citations to prior work on muscle mechanics and intrafusal fiber properties. Figure 4 shows the model architecture and demonstrates emergent cross-bridge dynamics. The approach is mechanistically grounded rather than phenomenological.

results.result: The biophysical model predicts that the scaling properties of muscle spindle dynamic responses and initial bursts with stretch velocity arise from intrafusal cross-bridge kinetics. The model exhibits sublinear (fractional-power) velocity scaling of dynamic index and linear acceleration scaling of initial burst amplitude, both emerging from the same mechanistic framework.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C49 demonstrate that classic velocity-dependent firing properties emerge from the cross-bridge model without explicit parameterization. Figure 5 shows quantitative agreement with classical experimental data for both velocity and acceleration scaling. The novelty claim (C49) appears valid based on the literature citations provided. The mechanistic explanation (strain-dependent detachment rates) is clearly articulated.

results.result: The biophysical model predicts history-dependent changes in muscle spindle firing (initial burst and dynamic response) analogous to those observed in multiple species. History dependence emerges from asymmetry in strain-dependent cross-bridge detachment rates, with recovery occurring over ~10 seconds. This is the first demonstration of history dependence in a muscle spindle model.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 show that the model reproduces history-dependent firing patterns observed across species (cat, rat, toad, human). Figure 6 demonstrates qualitative agreement with experimental data from multiple sources. While the model doesn't quantitatively match all details (acknowledged in C113), it captures the key phenomena. The novelty claim (C56) is supported by citations showing prior models lack this feature, though the mechanism was previously hypothesized (C55).

results.result: The biophysical model predicts differential effects of dynamic versus static gamma motor neuron activation on muscle spindle firing. Dynamic gamma drive increases initial burst and dynamic responses with smaller effects on baseline firing, while static gamma drive primarily increases baseline firing. These effects, including changes in dynamic index, match prior experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 and C91 demonstrate that gamma drive effects emerge from the biophysical model without explicit parameterization. Figure 7 shows quantitative predictions matching classical experimental findings. The model correctly predicts opposite effects on dynamic index for dynamic vs. static fiber activation. This validates that the model captures fusimotor control mechanisms through muscle mechanics alone.

results.result: During isometric conditions, the interaction between alpha drive (extrafusal muscle) and gamma drive (intrafusal muscle) produces highly variable muscle spindle firing patterns. Depending on the relative balance of alpha and gamma drive, Ia afferents can increase firing, decrease firing, or remain silent, explaining paradoxical observations in human experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C61-C72 demonstrate complex alpha-gamma interactions during isometric contractions. Figure 8 systematically shows how different combinations of drives produce diverse firing patterns, including the paradoxical human data from Edin & Vallbo (1990). The mechanistic explanation (extrafusal shortening vs. intrafusal activation) is clear and the simulations span the range of experimental observations. This addresses a longstanding puzzle in the field.

results.result: During muscle stretch with varying levels of alpha and gamma drive, muscle spindle firing depends on the interaction between musculotendon dynamics and intrafusal activation. Alpha drive reduces muscle spindle responses by causing extrafusal shortening, while gamma drive increases responses by activating intrafusal fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 demonstrate how alpha and gamma drive interact during muscle stretch. Figure 9 shows systematic effects on initial burst, dynamic response, and baseline firing. The results are internally consistent and mechanistically explained by the model structure. This extends the isometric findings to dynamic conditions.

results.result: The multiscale biophysical model demonstrates that diverse Ia afferent firing characteristics emerge from first principles of intrafusal muscle contractile mechanics. The model converts intrafusal force and yank into driving potentials via a simple linear relationship, representing the mechanotransduction process, and provides a framework for understanding proprioceptive signals across conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 summarize the main contributions of the work. The model successfully predicts multiple firing characteristics (history dependence, velocity scaling, gamma effects, alpha-gamma interactions) from biophysical principles without parameter changes across conditions. The framework is demonstrated to be more general than prior phenomenological models. The claim about providing a foundation for future work (C83) is reasonable given the demonstrated capabilities.

results.result: Depending on neuromechanical conditions, muscle spindle firing can appear to encode various biomechanical variables including force, yank, length, stiffness, velocity, and/or acceleration. The model reveals that firing depends critically on intrafusal fiber activation, force, and length, which shapes the degree to which firing resembles different extrafusal muscle variables.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C101, and C102 are supported by the diverse simulations showing context-dependent encoding properties. The model demonstrates how the same spindle can appear to encode different variables under different alpha-gamma activation patterns and mechanical conditions. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the apparent flexibility of muscle spindle encoding observed experimentally.

results.result: Muscle spindle Ia afferent firing exhibits movement history dependence and nonlinear scaling with stretch velocity. Firing patterns do not uniquely encode muscle length and velocity even in controlled conditions, and independent alpha and gamma activation can each profoundly alter sensory signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C6, and C7 establish well-known properties of muscle spindles that motivate the modeling work. These are supported by extensive citations to prior experimental literature and are consistent with the experimental data presented in the manuscript. These claims provide essential context for the significance of the modeling contributions.

results.result: Existing computational models of muscle spindle firing are largely phenomenological, have high fidelity under specific conditions but generalize poorly, and do not simulate history dependence. Prior models explicitly impose features like fractional-power velocity relationships rather than deriving them from biophysical principles.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C30, C31, C85, C88, and C89 provide a critical assessment of prior modeling approaches, supported by citations to existing models. The characterization of prior models as phenomenological and lacking history dependence is accurate based on the cited literature. This establishes the novelty and advantages of the current biophysical approach.

results.result: The anatomical arrangement and biomechanical properties of intrafusal muscle fibers affect muscle spindle firing. Muscle spindles contain specialized bag and chain fibers with similar basic architecture, innervated by gamma motor neurons in polar regions, with mechanotransduction occurring at the equatorial region. However, intrafusal forces have not been recorded with afferent activity, and few receptor potential recordings exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 and C32-C35 summarize established anatomical and physiological knowledge about muscle spindles, supported by extensive citations. The statements about experimental limitations (C12, C13) accurately describe gaps in the literature that motivate the modeling approach. This background is essential for understanding the model design.

results.result: The model design with slow-cycling myosin in the dynamic fiber and fast-cycling myosin in the static fiber, combined with structural modeling of intrafusal-extrafusal interactions, enables robust simulation of gamma drive effects. Variations in force and yank sensitivity account for static-dynamic variability across afferents and predict firing across different velocities and displacements.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 describe key model design choices and their consequences. The design is justified by citations to fiber properties (C92) and prior structural models (C93). The ability to account for afferent variability (C94, C96) and generalize across conditions (C97) is demonstrated in Figures 3 and 5. These are important validation results supporting the model's utility.

results.result: Explicit simulation of intrafusal muscle fibers within the muscle-tendon unit demonstrates profound effects of alpha and gamma drive during active conditions. This approach emphasizes the importance of anatomical arrangement shown in prior models and provides a computational testbed for exploring how intrafusal forces drive firing rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C100 describe the musculotendon modeling approach and its advantages. The importance of this structural approach is demonstrated in Figures 8 and 9. The comparison to prior work (C99) is supported by citations. The claim about providing a testbed (C100) is reasonable given the demonstrated capabilities, though somewhat speculative about future applications.

results.result: The model may explain complex Ia afferent behavior during locomotion, where firing appears to follow velocity/length during swing phase, increases during early stance despite no length change, and ceases during midstance. The model also addresses load-dependent firing in humans, potentially through agonist-antagonist interactions, though simulating intermuscular interactions would require coupled models.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C109 propose interpretations of locomotor and load-dependent firing based on the model, supported by citations to experimental observations. However, these specific scenarios were not actually simulated (acknowledged in the text). The interpretations are plausible given the model's demonstrated capabilities, but remain speculative without direct validation. The suggestion about intermuscular interactions (C108, C109) is reasonable but untested.

results.result: The model provides proof of concept for more elaborate models and can serve as a platform for testing effects of various multiscale mechanisms on muscle spindle firing. Future work could optimize parameters to match specific experimental conditions following approaches like Mileusnic et al. 2006.
results.evaluation: Claims C110, C111, and C122 describe the model's potential for future extensions. The proof-of-concept claim (C110) is supported by the demonstrated capabilities. The platform claim (C111) is reasonable given the modular structure, though the specific extensions listed are speculative. The suggestion about parameter optimization (C122) is a reasonable future direction supported by citation to prior work.

results.result: The model was designed to qualitatively reproduce history dependence using a simple two-state cross-bridge model. While it has limitations (cannot separate elastic contributions, discrepancies in triangle stretches, may not account for occlusion), it successfully reproduces sinusoidal stretch responses. Future improvements may require muscle-specific kinetics, sophisticated titin models, or accounting for additional history-dependence sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 provide an honest assessment of model limitations and potential improvements. The acknowledgment of qualitative vs. quantitative goals (C112) and specific shortcomings (C113, C114) is appropriate. The speculation about future improvements (C115, C116, C117) is reasonable and supported by citations. This critical self-assessment strengthens confidence in the supported claims.

results.result: Mechanotransduction mechanisms remain incompletely understood, so the model represents this process with constant gains. The dynamics of equatorial region viscoelasticity, ion channels, and intrinsic neural dynamics likely play significant roles not fully captured. The model framework could potentially extend to group II afferents and Golgi tendon organs.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 acknowledge limitations in modeling mechanotransduction and neural dynamics, supported by citations. The simplification to constant gains (C119) is clearly stated as a limitation. The recognition of unmodeled factors (C120) is appropriate and supported by literature. The speculation about extensions to other proprioceptors (C121) is reasonable but untested.

results.result: The complex interplay between central drive, internal forces, and environmental forces cannot be ignored when interpreting muscle spindle firing, especially during voluntary movement and environmental interactions. Neuromechanical interactions are key for understanding perception of force and position. The model provides a framework to move beyond viewing spindles as simple passive encoders.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C125 present the main conceptual conclusions of the work, supported by the modeling results and citations to prior work on perception (C124). The argument that spindles cannot be viewed as simple encoders is well-supported by the demonstrated context-dependent firing patterns. This represents an important conceptual advance in understanding proprioception.
